LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

Chicken — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson turns breakfast into the classroom: the chicken says cluck, the egg came from a hen, and the whole story gets told while the toast is still warm.

What is this?

A chicken is a farm bird that says cluck — a short ticking sound, easy to make, that pairs with the egg story every toddler’s kitchen already tells.

What does it mean?

Chicken–egg is a toddler’s first food chain: naming where breakfast comes from plants the seed of all later where-does-it-come-from thinking.

What does the child need to know?

Chicken, hen and rooster are three overlapping words; chicken is plenty at two. Keep the other two for later — the deck has a rooster card ready for the fancy version.

Why this matters

The cluck is quick to learn, and the egg link gives the word a daily slot at breakfast — a vocabulary word with a built-in reminder every single morning.

What it teaches

Everyday-connection thinking, sound imitation, and the first food-story words — egg, hen, breakfast — that later grow into real science talk.

Words to learn

chickencluckegghenfarmbreakfast

Say this to your child

“"A chicken! The chicken says cluck cluck. Can you cluck? Look — an egg! A hen laid this egg, and now it is our breakfast. Cluck cluck, thank you, hen."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and say chicken, then cluck cluck — quick little tick-tock noises.
  2. Peck like a chicken: finger beaks pecking at the palm, one cluck per peck. Your toddler’s hand will copy yours.
  3. At breakfast, hold the egg and tell the chain in your own words: "an egg comes from a hen — this one did, and now it is our breakfast." Then cluck once.
  4. When your toddler answers with a cuck, a kuk or just pecking fingers, peck back and add the word: chicken! Cluck!
  5. Cluck at breakfast every day this week — the egg moment makes the whole game self-restarting.

Look closer at the picture

The card shows a chicken saying cluck. Find the chicken, find the cluck, then ask what chickens lay — the egg is the story this card is here to tell.

Ask your child

"Where is the chicken?" "What does the chicken say?" "Who laid our breakfast egg?" "Can you peck like a chicken?"

What your child can say or do

"Cluck cluck!" or a beaky peck at your palm. Some toddlers will march the egg carton to the fridge announcing cluck — the food chain has taken up residence.

Out in the real world

Egg cartons, brunch menus and farm visits all replay this lesson. Carton in hand is the easiest: "eggs live here — a hen made these. Cluck!"

Try it together

Egg-and-spoon parade (a boiled egg, a big spoon, a short course across the rug): walk it, wobble it, rescue it. Clucking is mandatory, and the hen gets thanked at the finish line.

Understanding check

Ask what the chicken says and who lays eggs. A cluck plus an egg answer passes fully. If your toddler points at toast tomorrow and asks for a hen, take it as a distinction question and enjoy it.

Parent tips

Thank the hen out loud at breakfast — gratitude rituals glue vocabulary to routine better than any drill. Keep boiled eggs on hand; the parade is worth the prep.

Staying safe

Chicken-play eggs are boiled or plastic, never raw — raw shells splinter and raw egg is not for hands that go near mouths. Wash hands after any real farm contact, before snacks.

This lesson pairs with the Chicken flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Sounds (Toddler 5).
